archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose efficiency, point differential and passing game play like a winning side, but whose record has been dragged down by close losses, penalties and leaks on special teams and in the red zone.

report.headline: A plus point differential and a top-ten passing game hiding behind 3-6
report.take:
These are not the Texans of last year. In 2025 DeMeco Ryans had a defense-first 12-win team that allowed 17.4 points a game (2nd) and ranked 2nd in EPA allowed while the offense sat 22nd. This season has flipped. The offense is 8th in EPA, the passing game is 7th at 0.159 EPA per dropback, and C.J. Stroud has started every week with 2,462 passing yards behind a line that allows pressure on just 16.5% of dropbacks (4th). The defense has slid to 17th in EPA allowed and 24 points a game. It is now a team that wins by throwing, not by smothering.

The record lies about how well they have played. Houston has outscored opponents by 14 and is 13th in net EPA. Its point differential implies 4.8 wins, and its wins over expected (-1.82) rank 30th. Every loss except the 6-20 game against Cincinnati came by six points or fewer, and they have won only 20% of one-score games. That is mostly variance, but not all of it. They commit 8 penalties a game (23rd), the line is flagged 3.9 times a game (25th), special teams are 21st, the defense gives up touchdowns on 66.7% of red-zone trips (22nd), and they go for it on fourth down less than almost anyone (29th). Those are the details that decide three-point games, and they are habits as much as luck.

Two things in the numbers stand out. The pass rush is elite at finishing: 29 sacks (1st) and a 9.2% sack rate (2nd). But the defense behind it is all-or-nothing, 29th in explosive pass rate allowed and 24th on deep throws. It wins most downs (7th in success rate allowed) and then gives up the chunk play. The run game is broken at the point of attack: 3.32 yards a carry (28th) and 2.16 yards before contact (27th). That puts the problem on the line, not the backs, and it is why such a good passing game has stalled in some weeks.

The path forward is not hopeless. Jacksonville at 7-2 is running away with the division, so this is a wild-card chase. The schedule has soft spots: Indianapolis now, Washington, Philadelphia and Tennessee. A team this efficient should win more of its coin flips from here. The catch is health. Danielle Hunter and Azeez Al-Shaair are both out this week, and the defense was already leaning on its pass rush to cover for its leaks.

strengths.title: Stroud's passing game in a clean pocket
strengths.body: Houston is 7th in pass EPA. The protection is the reason it holds up: the line is 4th in pressure rate allowed and 5th in QB-hit rate, so Stroud gets to work the intermediate field on time. Pass protection is usually stickier than run blocking, so this should last, and the offense has topped 300 passing yards in big wins over Dallas, Jacksonville and the Chargers.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: The pressure rate is only middle of the pack (16th), but no team has more sacks and only one has a higher sack rate. When this front gets home, it gets the quarterback down, as in the eight-sack game against the Chargers. It also helps keep success rate allowed 7th. Losing Hunter tests how much of this is scheme and how much is him.

strengths.title: Underlying play beats the record
strengths.body: Net EPA ranks 13th, and the point differential implies close to five wins rather than three. Ball security has been good, with a +0.5 turnover margin per game (8th). Teams with this profile tend to see their close-game record drift back toward even.

concerns.title: The run game dies at the line
concerns.body: At 3.32 yards a carry, with almost no room before contact and a 33.7% run success rate (29th), Houston cannot lean on the ground to close games or convert short yardage (25th). This is a blocking problem, not a ball-carrier problem, so swapping Woody Marks for David Montgomery will not fix it on its own. It is the main reason a top-ten pass offense ranks only 17th in overall success rate.

concerns.title: Big plays allowed behind the rush
concerns.body: The defense wins a lot of individual downs, then gets beaten over the top: 29th in explosive pass rate and 24th in EPA on deep throws. Opposing WR2s score well above their usual output against it (30th). When the rush doesn't land, the coverage behind it is exposed, which is how Buffalo and Dallas each put up 334-plus passing yards.

concerns.title: Self-inflicted damage in close games
concerns.body: Eight penalties a game, below-average special teams and a leaky red-zone defense are the hidden yards that turned three-point games into losses. Cleveland, for one, came with 112 penalty yards. Some of the 20% one-score win rate is bad luck, but discipline is a coaching issue that won't fix itself.

trend.note: The passing game has been strong most weeks since Week 4, with double-digit pass EPA against Dallas, Jacksonville and the Chargers. Results have still swung week to week, including a home loss as a 10-point favorite to the Giants and a penalty-filled loss in Cleveland right after a 44-22 win.

nextGame.headline: Big favorite on a short week, but the Colts won in September
nextGame.body:
Houston is an 11.5-point home favorite (-650) on Thursday against a Colts offense that ranks 31st in EPA and dead last passing the ball under Daniel Jones. What Indianapolis does well is run: 6th in run EPA and 7th in run success. It also controls the clock (8th in time of possession) and has the better special teams (6th). Its defense is the worst in the league against the run by EPA, 27th in pressure rate and 31st in explosive pass rate allowed. Its saving grace is third downs, where it ranks 5th. Houston should not take that lightly: the Colts won the first meeting 19-17, holding Stroud to 167 passing yards even though Houston forced three turnovers.

Both sides are banged up on a four-day turnaround. Houston is without Danielle Hunter and Azeez Al-Shaair, its top linebacker by snaps. Woody Marks is doubtful with a concussion, which points to more David Montgomery, and Marvin Harrison Jr. is out. Indianapolis may be worse off. Tackle Jalen Travis is out and Bernhard Raimann is questionable in concussion protocol. Both starting corners, Charvarius Ward and Sauce Gardner, are questionable. Linebackers Akeem Davis-Gaither (IR) and Jaylon Carlies are out, along with two tight ends and the long snapper.

waysToWin.title: Pass rush feasts on patched tackles
waysToWin.body: Houston's sack rate is 2nd in the league. The Colts' line already ranks 28th in QB-hit rate allowed and may be playing without both starting tackles. Even without Hunter, sacks and hits on Jones should stall drives for the league's worst passing offense.

waysToWin.title: Stroud attacks a thin secondary
waysToWin.body: With Ward and Gardner both in doubt, the Colts rank 31st in explosive pass rate allowed and give up big EPA to WR3s and tight ends. That sets up Dalton Schultz and the slot. Houston's clean pocket gives Stroud time to find those matchups instead of forcing throws to the outside, where the Colts have been stingy against WR2s.

waysToWin.title: Finally a run game to close with
waysToWin.body: No defense allows more EPA per carry, and lead backs score well above their usual output against Indianapolis (32nd). The Colts are also missing two linebackers. If Montgomery can find yards here, Houston can protect a lead late instead of stalling as it did in its close losses.

waysToLose.title: Colts grind it on the ground
waysToLose.body: Indianapolis's run game is legitimately good. Houston is 21st in rush EPA allowed and gave up 188 rushing yards to the Giants. Without Al-Shaair and Hunter, the front is thinner. A long-drive, clock-heavy game limits Stroud's possessions and keeps the Colts close.

waysToLose.title: Losing the hidden-yardage battle
waysToLose.body: Houston averages 8 penalties a game, while the Colts are among the most disciplined teams (3rd). The special-teams gap runs the same way. In a game Vegas expects to be lopsided, flags and field position are the cleanest way for an underdog to stay within one score.

waysToLose.title: A September replay on third down
waysToLose.body: The Colts' defense is 5th on third down. In Week 3 it held Houston to 167 passing yards in a 19-17 upset. If Stroud is forced into third-and-long because the run game produces nothing, the offense can go cold again.

nextGame.watch: Houston's edge rush without Danielle Hunter against a Colts line that may be down both starting tackles.

restOfSeason.body:
The point differential and net EPA say this is roughly a .500-or-better team that has lost the close ones, and close-game records tend to drift back toward even. The passing game and protection look durable. The sack totals depend on Hunter getting healthy. The schedule splits cleanly. Indianapolis, Washington, Philadelphia and Tennessee are beatable, while Jacksonville, Pittsburgh and Green Bay will test a defense that gives up explosive plays. Expect Houston to win more often than it has, but without a real run game, the penalty habit and the red-zone defense will keep producing some frustrating losses.

What will likely regress: a takeaway count of 8 (25th) is low for a defense that sacks the quarterback this often, so more turnovers should come. The one-score record should also improve. What probably won't change much: the run blocking, and the defense's tendency to give up the deep ball. A finish around 8 or 9 wins puts them on the wild-card bubble, not in the division race.
swingFactors: Danielle Hunter's and Azeez Al-Shaair's return
Whether close games stop going the other way
Run blocking enough to protect leads

confidence.note: Nine games, and a clear gap between efficiency and record, but key defensive injuries cloud the next few weeks.
